## What to see in Uruguay: cities, coastline, and wineries

For a first trip to [Uruguay](/uruguay/), choose several different experiences. [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) introduces the modern capital and historic neighborhoods; [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) offers colonial architecture beside the Río de la Plata; and [Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/) is known for seaside relaxation. Wineries and smaller towns can be added to one of these main destinations.

Our collection includes {{catalog.placesCountPhrase}}. The key is to distribute your days among cities, history, beaches, and gastronomy rather than trying to visit every point in a row.

## Montevideo: history within one city

[Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) makes a convenient starting point. It has an international airport, museums, markets, and restaurants, while the long Rambla promenade follows the shore. In the center, you can combine [Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/) with [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/), its architecture, and its cafes.

To understand the character of this port capital, visit the [Port of Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/) and [Metropolitan Cathedral](/uruguay/place/montevideo-cathedral/). Both fit naturally into a historic-center walk, leaving time for lunch. A relaxed day on foot reveals much more of city life than a series of short stops seen through a car window.

For food and wine experiences near the capital, consider estates such as [Bouza Winery](/uruguay/place/bouza-winery/) and [Spinoglio](/uruguay/place/spinoglio-winery/). Compare not only the wine brands but also whether tours, tastings, lunch, and transfers are available. Each winery has its own visitor arrangements.

## Colonia del Sacramento and western Uruguay

[Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) is known for its UNESCO-listed historic quarter. Cobblestone streets, low houses, the remains of fortifications, and views across the Río de la Plata explain why travelers come to walk rather than to visit a long series of large museums.

Colonia is also convenient when traveling between Uruguay and Argentina, but ferry schedules, luggage arrangements, and connections need checking for the specific date. Its location beside the water does not guarantee a suitable sailing at every hour.

To explore Uruguay's industrial history, visit [Fray Bentos](/uruguay/place/fray-bentos/) on the Uruguay River. It is known for its meat-processing industrial heritage, represented in a UNESCO World Heritage property. This is a separate journey for travelers interested in labor, production, and river-town history.

## Atlantic coast: resorts or quieter stops

[Punta del Este](/uruguay/place/punta-del-este/) attracts visitors for its beaches, waterfronts, restaurants, and ocean walks. Nearby [Punta Ballena](/uruguay/place/punta-ballena/) offers sweeping coastal views. [Piriápolis](/uruguay/place/piriapolis/) offers a different holiday style, with seaside walks and green hills.

| Destination | Main appeal |
|---|---|
| Punta del Este | Beaches and a lively resort town |
| Punta Ballena | Coastal panoramas |
| Piriápolis | Relaxed walks by the sea |

The Southern Hemisphere summer months are generally more suitable for a conventional beach trip, while the coast is quieter outside the peak season. Water and wind conditions matter even on sunny days, especially for independent water activities.

## Wine, nature, and additional stops

Winemaking thrives in [Canelones](/uruguay/place/canelones/), including Uruguay's characteristic Tannat grape. Beyond estates near the capital, [Garzón Winery](/uruguay/place/garzon-winery/) in the east deserves attention. When planning a tasting, take account of the winery's location, advance reservations, and transport arrangements.

For a quieter introduction to regional history, visit [San Javier](/uruguay/place/san-javier/), associated in part with Russian-speaking settlers. Choose such a trip according to your interests, as the town lies away from the main Montevideo–Colonia–Punta del Este route.

## Planning a route without unnecessary transfers

Choose your combination according to your goals:

| Time and priority | Suggested option |
|---|---|
| Short stay | Montevideo and one nearby stop |
| History and architecture | Montevideo + Colonia |
| Beaches and relaxation | Punta del Este + coast |
| Wine and cuisine | Montevideo + wineries |

If you are continuing to Argentina or Brazil, check not just geographic proximity but the actual order of connections. Our [Uruguay tours](/uruguay/tour/) include programs with different countries and services; the individual tour pages show which cities are genuinely included.

## Frequently asked questions about places in Uruguay

### Montevideo or Colonia for a first visit?

For city museums, markets, and restaurants, choose Montevideo. Colonia is more attractive if you want colonial streets and several hours beside the Río de la Plata. If you have enough time, the two complement each other.

### Where should I stay for beaches?

Punta del Este is one of the principal resort choices. A quieter holiday can focus on Piriápolis or other coastal areas, choosing a beach according to season and expected conditions.

### Can I visit wineries without my own car?

Yes, with an agreed transfer or organized excursion. Check opening arrangements and tasting conditions before buying the trip.

## Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral: the church on Plaza Matriz

Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral (Catedral Metropolitana de Montevideo), also known as Iglesia Matriz, stands in Uruguay's historic capital district, [Ciudad Vieja](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/). Its pale facade with two towers faces Constitution Square, usually called Plaza Matriz by local residents. Old civic buildings and walking routes through the center surround it.

This is an important monument to the city's colonial and republican history. It is worth visiting for more than religious reasons: the cathedral helps show how Montevideo grew from a small fortified settlement into the capital of an independent state.

## Cathedral history: from colonial church to archbishop's seat

Construction of the present building began in 1790 on the site of an earlier church. The new church was consecrated in 1804, while the area remained under Spanish colonial rule. The church's status changed at the end of the 19th century: in 1897, Pope Leo XIII elevated it to the cathedral of the Archdiocese of Montevideo.

Its history reflects that of the country. The square in front of the church was an important urban space long before today's wide capital avenues appeared. Religious and civic events took place here, colonial administrative institutions stood nearby, and the purposes of the surrounding public spaces changed after independence.

The cathedral is designated a national historic monument. It remains both a functioning religious building and an architectural heritage site.

## Architecture and details worth noticing

### Neoclassical facade

The main facade follows a restrained Neoclassical style. Two towers frame the center, while columns and a pediment create clear symmetry. This architectural language differs from the more elaborate Baroque churches found in other Latin American cities.

For photographs, step back onto the square to appreciate the building's proportions. Also examine the portal, windows, towers, and neighboring buildings to understand how the cathedral relates to the historic square.

### Interior and religious heritage

The interior retains the solemn character of a church. Worship services and important ceremonies are still held here, so visits must respect its religious purpose.

When the cathedral is open, take a quiet look at the interior, altar area, and commemorative architectural details. Photography and access to individual areas depend on current rules and worship schedules. Speak quietly and respect people attending services.

## Plaza Matriz and old Montevideo

Constitution Square (Plaza Constitución, or Plaza Matriz) is one of the city's historic squares. It was the central plaza of fortified colonial Montevideo. Opposite the cathedral stands the old Cabildo, a building that housed different municipal institutions over time.

The square shows two important institutions of the earlier city: religious and administrative. During the 19th century, the open space changed, with new paths, trees, and civic features added. Today it offers a pleasant break during a walk through the historic center.

Nearby Sarandí pedestrian street is one of the main routes through [Montevideo's Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/). After exploring the cathedral, continue toward Independence Square or the port districts.

## Including the cathedral in a Ciudad Vieja walk

A convenient route begins at [Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/). From there, pass through the old Citadel Gate onto pedestrian Sarandí Street and continue to Plaza Matriz. After visiting the cathedral and Cabildo, explore more of the historic quarters and the [Port of Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/).

For a brief introduction, the facade and square are enough. If you are interested in religious history or architecture, allow time for the interior and neighboring buildings. The actual duration depends on which museums and public spaces are included.

Montevideo's tourism portal gives the cathedral's address as Ituzaingó 1373. Access may change during services and events, so confirm opening arrangements before your visit.

## Montevideo Cathedral on Ada Tours itineraries

The cathedral appears in an optional day trip to Montevideo offered on our ["Best of Argentina: 14 Days with Bariloche and Iguazu" tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/). This is **an optional excursion**, not a mandatory part of the main Argentina itinerary. Travelers cross the Río de la Plata by ferry and see the port, [Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/), Old Town, and cathedral.

If you want to get to know Uruguay's capital independently of a larger tour, start with our general [Montevideo destination page](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) and choose a walk through its historic districts.

## Frequently asked questions about Montevideo Cathedral

### Is the cathedral in the modern center or Old Town?

It is in [Ciudad Vieja](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/), the historic district of Montevideo, on Constitution Square, also known as Plaza Matriz.

### When was the present building constructed?

Construction began in 1790, and the church was consecrated in 1804. It became a cathedral in 1897.

### Can I go inside?

It is an active cathedral, open for religious use and visits during designated hours. Check access before going and take worship times into account.

### How much time should I spend around the cathedral?

The facade and square make a short stop. Add the Cabildo, neighboring historic buildings, and Sarandí Street, and it is better to allow several hours for [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/).

## Montevideo Cathedral as part of an optional excursion

[Montevideo Metropolitan Cathedral](/uruguay/place/montevideo-cathedral/) is in historic Ciudad Vieja near Plaza Matriz. Its two-towered, Neoclassical facade faces one of the city's oldest squares. Work on the current building began in the late 18th century, and it acquired cathedral status in the 19th century.

You can see it on a [day trip to Montevideo from Buenos Aires](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/). But on the tours discussed here, this is **an optional visit** involving a journey into another country. A standalone mandatory day devoted exclusively to the cathedral is not offered.

This matters when planning. The cathedral is visited during a broader guided tour of Uruguay's capital; the whole day also includes transfers, a ferry crossing, and a return to Argentina.

## Which tours offer this option?

On the [14-day "Best of Argentina: Bariloche and Iguazu" tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), a free day in Buenos Aires may be used for a trip to Montevideo. The main program covers the Argentine capital, Patagonia, Bariloche, and Iguazu Falls. Uruguay is a separate choice and should not be counted as a mandatory part of this itinerary.

The [10-day "Brazil, Argentina and Chile: Champions Parade, Tango and Wine" tour](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/) also offers an optional Montevideo excursion during one of its Buenos Aires days. The trip has a different theme: festive events in Brazil and visits to several countries. The extra day in Uruguay therefore needs to fit around the other scheduled activities.

| Tour | Role of the excursion |
|---|---|
| Argentina in 14 days | An alternative use of a free day |
| Champions Parade, 10 days | A separate excursion from Buenos Aires |

Both options involve **sightseeing in Montevideo as a whole**. The cathedral is one stop on the wider route, alongside the port, Independence Square, and Old Town. Travelers primarily interested in museums and architecture should assess the amount of free time; those hoping to see Uruguay in a day will get a first introduction to the capital.

## How the excursion day unfolds

On the [Ada Tours day trip](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/), travelers are taken to the Buenos Aires terminal in the morning. They then cross the Río de la Plata by ferry, meet a guide, and explore Montevideo. The route passes through the port, Independence Square, the city center, and Old Town.

These historic sites are linked by one walking route. In the [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/) area, visitors can see historic facades and reach [Metropolitan Cathedral](/uruguay/place/montevideo-cathedral/). Its position on Plaza Matriz makes it a natural stop in the historic center. Free time follows the city tour, then travelers take the return ferry to Buenos Aires and transfer to their hotel.

The cathedral's mention in an itinerary should not be equated with a guaranteed extended interior visit. It is a functioning church, so access may depend on services, official opening hours, and the pace of the excursion. **The route includes the cathedral as a stop**, not a separately confirmed private tour of its interior.

## What can you learn during a brief cathedral stop?

The cathedral is linked to old Montevideo, which developed around the fortified town and central square. Nearby pedestrian streets in Ciudad Vieja bring together religious architecture, former administrative buildings, and later city development.

During a short stop, focus on the facade, towers, and relationship to the square. If time and visiting rules permit, the interior offers more, but an unarranged interior tour is not part of the confirmed services.

History enthusiasts will find it more rewarding to view the cathedral in the context of [historic Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/), rather than as the sole purpose of the day. If your main interest is colonial architecture and a quieter walk, another option from Buenos Aires is the [Colonia del Sacramento excursion](/uruguay/colonia-del-sacramento/colonia-del-sacramento-from-buenos-aires/). It is a different town with a different itinerary.

## What to arrange before adding Uruguay

The ferry crossing turns an ordinary free day into international travel. Confirm outbound and return sailings, transfers in the Argentine capital, the chosen excursion format, and guiding language. Group and private versions of the Montevideo excursion are available in both the fourteen- and ten-day tour programs; check the exact services and price in the itinerary.

Entry to Uruguay and re-entry to Argentina also require checking travel documents for the relevant citizenship and dates. Do not assume that requirements are identical for every passport. If a domestic or international flight is scheduled for the following day, consider the time buffer and fatigue after a full sightseeing day.

The cathedral is especially interesting to travelers who enjoy architecture, religious history, and city walks. Visiting it need not turn an entire South American journey into a specialized history tour: you can choose one suitable free day. But if rest between flights or preparation for a busy festive program matters more, you can skip the optional outing.

## Frequently asked questions about Montevideo Cathedral on tours

### Is Montevideo Cathedral included in the main itinerary?

No. On the [14-day Argentina tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/) and [10-day Champions Parade program](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/), the cathedral appears as part of an optional excursion to Uruguay's capital.

### Can I enter the cathedral during the excursion?

It depends on the agreed route, arrival time, and operating schedule of the active church. The current programs include the cathedral as a sightseeing stop, but do not promise an extended interior tour.

### Do I need to stay overnight in Montevideo?

The [excursion from Buenos Aires](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/) returns to Argentina on the same day. A night in Montevideo is not specified as mandatory for this extra excursion.

### How does Montevideo differ from Colonia?

Montevideo introduces the capital, its squares and Old Town, including the cathedral. [Colonia del Sacramento](/uruguay/place/colonia-del-sacramento/) is best known for its historic architecture and walking through a smaller town. Choose according to which experience matters most during your free day.

## Independence Square in Montevideo: from the Citadel Gate to the Artigas monument

Independence Square (Plaza Independencia) lies between historic [Montevideo Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/) and the city's central districts. It is one of Uruguay's principal squares. An equestrian statue of José Gervasio Artigas rises in the center, the old Citadel Gate stands at the western edge, and Salvo Palace and important civic buildings surround the space.

For first-time visitors to [Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/), the square is a convenient place to trace the city's expansion from a colonial fortress to the capital of an independent country. The sites stand close together, so even a short stop reveals several historical periods.

## Why is the square between Old Town and the newer center?

In colonial times, Montevideo was a fortified town with gates and defensive works. After independence and the demolition of much of its fortifications, the cleared space became available for new urban planning. Architect Carlo Zucchi designed the square in 1837. It became a link between Ciudad Vieja and the expanding city center.

Montevideo's municipal photography archive records that the square acquired its modern outline by 1877. Its appearance changed as the city grew, with monuments, palaces, and administrative buildings added. Today the contrast between the historic gate and later architecture is especially apparent.

To the east begins 18 de Julio Avenue, one of the city's main streets. To the west, the old Citadel Gate leads into [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/).

## What to see at Independence Square

### Monument to José Artigas and his mausoleum

The equestrian statue at the center honors José Gervasio Artigas, a national hero of Uruguay and one of the leaders of the region's 19th-century struggle for political self-determination. The sculpture, by Italian artist Angelo Zanelli, was installed in 1923.

Beneath the monument is a mausoleum opened in 1977, where Artigas's remains rest. It demonstrates his place in national memory: the square is a setting for state ceremonies as well as everyday urban life.

Access to the mausoleum's interior depends on visiting rules and hours. Even if it is closed, the statue and surrounding square can still be appreciated from outside.

### Citadel Gate

Puerta de la Ciudadela is a surviving fragment of Montevideo's colonial fortifications. People once passed through this gate into the old citadel. It recalls a town defended by walls, a moat, and military infrastructure.

Its current position reflects a history of dismantling, storage, and return. Municipal archives note that the gate was moved and then restored to its former position in 1959. It is a good place to begin a walk along pedestrian Sarandí Street toward other landmarks in historic Montevideo.

### Salvo Palace and surrounding buildings

Palacio Salvo occupies a prominent site on the square's eastern side. Opened in 1928, its silhouette became a familiar part of the city center. Nearby stand the former Estévez Presidential Palace and the modern Executive Tower.

Solís Theatre, one of the capital's cultural landmarks, is also close to the square. For a brief visit, seeing the architecture from outside is enough; interior tours, observation decks, and museum visits should be planned separately.

## Walking route from the square

A convenient independent walk follows the Artigas monument, Citadel Gate, pedestrian Sarandí Street, the historic neighborhoods of [Ciudad Vieja](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/), and [Metropolitan Cathedral](/uruguay/place/montevideo-cathedral/). It reveals the transition from an official national square to more intimate old city streets.

If you arrive at the [Port of Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/), the square is often one of the first stops on a sightseeing route. The port, square, and cathedral each deserve time; plan your stops rather than simply driving past them.

For photographs, the broad view toward Artigas's statue and the silhouette of Salvo Palace are especially distinctive. Daylight helps reveal facade details, while evening illumination brings out the architecture in another way. Comfortable shoes are useful for a longer walk on cobbled and pedestrian streets.

## Independence Square on Ada Tours excursions

Our [Montevideo excursion from Buenos Aires](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/) includes Independence Square along with the [port](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/), central districts, Old Town, and the cathedral. It provides a first look at the capital's main historic stops in a single ferry day.

On the ["Best of Argentina: 14 Days" tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), the outing is offered as an optional excursion, with its own terms and price. Uruguay's appearance in a tour's geography does not mean that the excursion is included in the basic package.

If you enjoy history and architecture, make the square a priority. Extra time is needed for the waterfront, museums, or a separate theater visit.

## How Independence Square differs from Plaza Matriz

These are two distinct urban spaces. Independence Square symbolizes the country's emergence as an independent nation and connects Old Town to newer districts. Historic Plaza Matriz lies deeper in Ciudad Vieja near the cathedral and is associated with earlier city life.

Both squares can be seen in one walk, but their surroundings and histories differ. Moving between them reveals Montevideo's evolution from a fortified port into a modern city.

## Frequently asked questions about Independence Square

### Where is Independence Square?

In central Montevideo, between Ciudad Vieja and 18 de Julio Avenue. Pedestrian streets connect it with [Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/).

### Who is depicted in the monument?

José Gervasio Artigas, Uruguay's national hero. A mausoleum dedicated to him stands beneath the statue.

### What is the Citadel Gate?

It is a surviving historic gate from Montevideo's former colonial fortifications, symbolizing the entrance to the old citadel.

### Can I visit the square in one day from Buenos Aires?

Yes. The square is included in the [Ada Tours Montevideo day trip](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/) by ferry. The time available for independent walking depends on the schedule of the chosen excursion.

## Independence Square as an optional stop in Montevideo

[Independence Square](/uruguay/place/montevideo-independence-square/) connects Montevideo's central streets with historic Ciudad Vieja. It is home to the equestrian monument to José Gervasio Artigas, the gate of the former citadel, and Salvo Palace. For travelers arriving from Argentina for one day, it is an ideal starting point for discovering Uruguay's capital.

The square appears on our [Montevideo day trip from Buenos Aires](/uruguay/montevideo/montevideo-day-trip-from-buenos-aires/). On two larger Ada Tours itineraries, the excursion is **optional**: it can be added by agreement but is not part of the mandatory program. This selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with that possibility.

## What to see around the square

The monument to Artigas stands in the center, with a mausoleum below. At the western end is the Citadel Gate, a historic entrance toward [Montevideo Old Town](/uruguay/place/montevideo-old-town/). The square's development reflects the city's 19th-century expansion beyond its colonial fortifications.

Several eras are visible together: the Citadel Gate recalls colonial Montevideo, while Salvo Palace and the surrounding buildings belong to later chapters in the city's history. Solís Theatre is nearby. A sightseeing tour lets visitors see this architecture from outside, but **admission to the theater, mausoleum, and museums should not be considered included without separate confirmation**.

From the square, Sarandí pedestrian street leads into the old districts. Even a short walk gives a sense of the historic center. If you want to spend more time here, remember the return ferry schedule: sightseeing and free time must both fit into one excursion day.

## Tours on which the square can be added

On the [14-day "Best of Argentina" itinerary](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), the main route runs through Buenos Aires, El Calafate, Ushuaia, Bariloche, and Iguazu. An optional day trip to Montevideo is offered from Buenos Aires. Uruguay and Independence Square are additional visits, not part of the main itinerary.

On the [10-day "Champions Parade, Tango and Wine" journey](/multi-country/tour/brazil-argentina-chile-champions-parade-10-days-2027/), the main countries are Brazil, Argentina, and Chile. Uruguay can likewise be added from Buenos Aires. However, the busy schedule of parades, excursions, and transfers means the free day must be agreed; the additional trip does not replace scheduled events.

Both tours offer two Montevideo excursion options: **$500 per person** in a shared group with an English-speaking guide, or **$850 per person** privately with a Russian-speaking guide, for at least two participants. Ferry tickets are included in the price of this optional excursion. Exact dates and availability must be agreed when choosing the main tour.

## A day across the Río de la Plata

The day starts with an early transfer to the Buenos Aires ferry terminal. Travelers cross the Río de la Plata, meet a guide at the [Port of Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo-port/), and tour the capital. The route covers Independence Square, central streets, Old Town, and [Metropolitan Cathedral](/uruguay/place/montevideo-cathedral/). There is free time afterward, followed by a return ferry and transfer to the hotel in Buenos Aires.

Allow time for border formalities and check-in before boarding. Sailing schedules, luggage conditions, and entry documents must be checked for the actual service and each traveler's citizenship. Do not plan another long excursion from Buenos Aires on the same day without prior agreement.

## When visiting the square must be part of the main itinerary

The [20-day six-country Latin America tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) and [32-day eight-country itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) include Montevideo on their principal routes. In these journeys, the ferry and city sightseeing form part of the scheduled program. They belong to the [tours through Montevideo](/uruguay/place/montevideo/tour/) rather than the catalog of optional visits to Independence Square.

For a more extended stay in the capital and other areas, compare [Uruguay tours](/uruguay/tour/), where the country is more than a day trip from Argentina.

## Frequently asked questions about optional visits to Independence Square

### Is Independence Square included in the basic fourteen-day tour?

No. On the ["Best of Argentina" tour](/multi-country/tour/best-of-argentina-14-days/), it is part of a separately paid Montevideo excursion.

### Do ferry tickets cost extra?

Ferry tickets are included in the stated price of the optional excursion. The excursion itself is not included in the base rate of the two tours discussed.

### Can I see the square and Old Town in one day?

Yes. Both are part of the same sightseeing route. Museum admission and walking time depend on the agreed itinerary and return ferry schedule.

### Which tours already include Montevideo?

See the [20-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) and [32-day journey](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/). The city is included in their main programs.
